La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: The Hunger (1983) Role
facts.body: David Bowie starred as an elegant vampire in the 1983 movie *The Hunger*, which became a favorite among Goth enthusiasts. The film also featured a nightclub scene with Bauhaus performing "Bela Lugosi's Dead." "Bowie starred as a rather elegant vampire in a movie called The Hunger back in 1983."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Good Goth: Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: $17.5 Million EMI Record Deal - 1983
facts.body: In 1983, Bowie secured a monumental $17.5 million record deal with EMI Records, one of the largest in the industry at that time. In exchange, he committed to creating a more commercially accessible album. "And then there was the new 17.5 million dollar record deal with EMI Records, one of the biggest deals in the industry to that time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: MTV Racism Challenge (1983)
facts.body: In 1983, David Bowie confronted MTV VJ Mark Goodman in an interview, calling out the channel's "subtle racism" for featuring very few Black artists, particularly during prime daytime hours. He observed that while many Black artists were making excellent videos, they were rarely aired on MTV, in contrast to a dedicated Black music station. "I'm just flawed by the fact that there's so many so few black artists featured on it. Why is that?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "Let's Dance" Birth from Acoustic Guitar (1983)
facts.body: The massive hit "Let's Dance" originated from a simple tune Bowie had written on an acoustic guitar. Nile Rogers then transformed it by adding syncopation, turning it into a "bang" and a signature glossy new romantic new wave track. "Rogers took a simple tune Bowie had written on an acoustic guitar, added syncopation, and turned it into a bang."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "China Girl" Royalties for Iggy Pop (1983)
facts.body: Bowie's decision to cover "China Girl," a song he co-wrote for Iggy Pop's 1977 album "The Idiot," was partly an act of friendship. Iggy Pop's finances were described as "shaky" in the early 80s, and Bowie knew the royalties from the hit cover would provide a significant windfall for him. "Legend has it, Bowie wanted to do his friend Iggy Pop a favor by covering the song. Iggy's finances in the early 80s were shaky, and Bowie knew the royalties from a China Girl cover would be a windfall."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "China Girl" Music Video Controversy (1983)
facts.body: The music video for "China Girl" was considered risque, satirizing Asian stereotypes and concluding with Bowie and actress Geeling Ng recreating the fully nude crashing waves embrace from the 1950s film "From Here to Eternity." The controversy surrounding the video likely contributed to the song's commercial success. "fueled by a risque music video that satirized Asian stereotypes and closed with Bowie recreating the crashing waves embrace from the 50s film from here to eternity, with actress Gilling Eng, both fully nude in the surf."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "Serious Moonlight" Tour Image (1983)
facts.body: During his "Serious Moonlight" tour, captured in the "Modern Love" music video, Bowie appeared as a sleek, "up-ified pop idol," dressed in a yellow suit with blonde hair teased into a Little Richard-style pompadour. This image was part of his mid-80s "imperial phase" persona, reflecting his embrace of mainstream pop stardom. "captured Bowie live on stage on his just launched Sirius Moonlight tour, Natalie dressed in a yellow suit, his blonde hair teased into a little Richard style pompadour, tricked out like a sleek, up-ified pop idol."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: "China Girl" Royalties for Iggy Pop (1983)
facts.body: Bowie's decision to cover "China Girl," a song he co-wrote for Iggy Pop's 1977 album "The Idiot," was partly an act of friendship. Iggy Pop's finances were described as "shaky" in the early 80s, and Bowie knew the royalties from the hit cover would provide a significant windfall for him. "Legend has it, Bowie wanted to do his friend Iggy Pop a favor by covering the song. Iggy's finances in the early 80s were shaky, and Bowie knew the royalties from a China Girl cover would be a windfall."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "China Girl" Music Video Controversy (1983)
facts.body: The music video for "China Girl" was considered risque, satirizing Asian stereotypes and concluding with Bowie and actress Geeling Ng recreating the fully nude crashing waves embrace from the 1950s film "From Here to Eternity." The controversy surrounding the video likely contributed to the song's commercial success. "fueled by a risque music video that satirized Asian stereotypes and closed with Bowie recreating the crashing waves embrace from the 50s film from here to eternity, with actress Gilling Eng, both fully nude in the surf."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "Serious Moonlight" Tour Image (1983)
facts.body: During his "Serious Moonlight" tour, captured in the "Modern Love" music video, Bowie appeared as a sleek, "up-ified pop idol," dressed in a yellow suit with blonde hair teased into a Little Richard-style pompadour. This image was part of his mid-80s "imperial phase" persona, reflecting his embrace of mainstream pop stardom. "captured Bowie live on stage on his just launched Sirius Moonlight tour, Natalie dressed in a yellow suit, his blonde hair teased into a little Richard style pompadour, tricked out like a sleek, up-ified pop idol."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Initial CD Releases and Liner Notes (1983)
facts.body: When CDs first launched in 1983, initial releases, including some of The Beatles' albums, often came with "wretched" and uninspired liner note booklets. These early CD packages frequently featured minimal content, sometimes just a small piece of glossy paper with one side blank, falling short of the detailed liner notes seen on vinyl LPs. "Some of the first Beatles albums released on CD came this way."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Digital Debris  Part 3: Liner Notes
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Delayed Adoption of CD Format (1983-1987)
facts.body: When compact discs emerged in early 1983, The Beatles' organization was highly cautious, delaying their entry into the new format until early 1987 to observe its market development and stability. "When the compact disc started showing up in stores in early 1983, the Beatles would have none of this new format."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

facts.title: Fractured Skull Attack (August 1983) – Street Brawl Led to Brain Surgery, Later Distrust of Doctors, and Death
facts.body: In August 1983, Johnny Ramone became involved in a brawl with Seth Maclin of a band called Sub Zero Construction on the street outside Johnny's East Village apartment at 4am. Johnny was beaten to the pavement and kicked in the head. He was rushed to hospital with a fractured skull and required brain surgery. He recovered, but the incident left him deeply distrustful of doctors. When he later began experiencing abdominal pain — roughly 15 years after the attack — his mistrust caused him to delay seeking treatment. The abdominal pain was aggressive prostate cancer that spread throughout his body. Chemotherapy failed, and Johnny died on September 15, 2004. "Had he not been beaten up in the summer of 1983 and still trusted doctors?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 7
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.body: By 1983, and definitively by 1984, hip hop had fully established its distinct identity, encompassing the cultures of breakbeat and sampling. facts.title: Second British Invasion Impact (1983-1984)
facts.body: Starting in 1982 and 1983, British New Wave bands, along with New Romantic groups, transitioned from "curios" to "video superstars" and "chart conquerors" in America by 1984. Fuelled by MTV, these movements, exemplified by acts like Duran Duran and Eurythmics, "redefined the cutting edge of cool" in the US. "The bands that had benefited the most from the rise of the music video in America were British New Romantic and New Wave bands, who, starting in 1982 and 83, went from Curios in America to Viva."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1

facts.title: Firing of Mick Jones (September 1, 1983) – Manager-Engineered Split That Destroyed the Band
facts.body: Manager Bernie Rhodes had spent years pitting Joe Strummer against Mick Jones, encouraging Joe to fire him. On September 1, 1983, Mick Jones's departure was announced in a formal "Clash Communiqué" stating he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the Clash." The resulting lineup recorded the critically panned *Cut the Crap* (1985), featuring two new members, after which the Clash simply dissolved with no official announcement. Mick Jones went on to major success with Big Audio Dynamite, while Strummer spent over a decade in record-company limbo and never again achieved the stature he had with the Clash. "Firing Mick Jones? Terrible. Joe Strummer thought he knew better than Mick, and he ended up paying for it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 10 Terrible Career Moves
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Mick Jones' Dismissal (September 1, 1983)
facts.body: Guitarist Mick Jones was fired on September 1, 1983, a decision announced via a "clash communique" that stated he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the clash." This followed increasing difficulties, including being late for rehearsals and recording, refusing tours, and his relationship with Joe Strummer deteriorating due to Bernie Rhodes's machinations. Joe Strummer expressed frustration about having to "beg him to play the guitar," comparing the situation to "dragging a dead dog around." "It was September 1st, 1983, and his firing was announced in what was called a clash communique."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: You're Fired!
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Mick Jones's Firing (September 1983)
facts.body: In September 1983, Joe Strummer orchestrated what was described as a "coup" by issuing an "infamous clash communique," essentially firing Mick Jones, who had co-founded The Clash in 1976. Joe expressed frustration with Mick's perceived lack of commitment, stating he had to "beg him to play the guitar" and comparing the situation to "dragging a dead dog around on a bit of string." This decision was widely seen as detrimental, and The Clash "was never the same after Mick left."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Joe Strummer: A Remembrance
facts.name: The Clash

facts.body: In 1983, Paul McCartney advised Michael Jackson on the lucrative nature of publishing, famously telling him, "He who owns the publishing controls the world." This advice significantly influenced Jackson. "The money is in publishing, Mac and console Jacko. He who owns the publishing controls the world. And this was advice that Jackson never forgot."

facts.title: MTV Color Barrier Challenge (1983)
facts.body: In the early years of MTV, Michael Jackson, despite his fame, faced difficulty getting his videos aired due to the channel's initial policy of showing almost exclusively rock and pop from white artists. This subtle racism greatly annoyed David Bowie, who publicly challenged MTV on the issue during a 1983 interview. The channel eventually relented after CBS Records threatened to pull all its videos, leading to Jackson's "Thriller" videos breaking the color barrier. "If you were a black artist, the chances of you getting on MTV were zilch. Even if your name was Michael Jackson, which greatly annoyed David Bowie."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

facts.title: Pre-NIN New Wave Bands (1983) – Option 30 and Others Disowned After Fame
facts.body: Before Nine Inch Nails, Trent Reznor played in several bands based in the Cleveland, Ohio area that released recordings and sounded markedly different — far softer and more new wave — than the industrial sound he later became known for. One group, called Option 30, recorded new wave material in 1983. After NIN broke through in the late 1980s, Trent reportedly had his sister scour record stores in eastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania to buy up all remaining copies of these earlier recordings, in an effort to erase evidence of that part of his career. "Trent did try to disown that part of his musical past."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Dave Mustaine's Firing (April 11, 1983)
facts.body: Dave Mustaine was fired from Metallica on April 11, 1983, after two years with the band, due to his excessive alcohol and drug use, coupled with aggressive behavior. Key incidents included a physical altercation after his dog scratched bassist Ron McGovney's car, and an incident where he poured beer into McGovney's bass, causing a severe electric shock. The final catalyst was his "out of control" behavior during album recording in New York, leading the band to pack his gear, drive him to the Port Authority bus terminal, give him a ticket, and tell him not to return. "The packed up all his gear, drove him to the Port Authority bus terminal, gave him a ticket and said, don't ever come back. That was April 11, 1983."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: You're Fired!
facts.name: Metallica

facts.title: Band Breakup - Hammersmith Palais (1983)
facts.body: Bauhaus concluded their initial run with a final performance on July 5, 1983, at the Hammersmith Palais in London. The breakup was attributed to rising egos, creative differences, the pressures of touring, and Peter Murphy's severe bout of pneumonia, which forced the band to record an album without him, leading to internal divisions. "As the gig at the Hammersmith Pele came to an end, David J grabbed the mic and said, rest in peace. And that was that. Bajaos was dead."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Courtney Love Briefly Auditioned (1983); Chuck Mosley Fired After Falling Asleep at Showcase; Mike Patton Took Over
facts.body: Faith No More evolved from a band called Sharp Young Men, eventually cycling through several singers, including an approximately 20-minute audition by Courtney Love sometime in 1983. Chuck Mosley served as singer from 1983 and recorded their first two albums, but was fired in 1988 after getting into fights with bandmates and roadies, refusing to do anything but acoustic sets, and — most critically — falling asleep on stage during an important showcase performance. His replacement was Mike Patton, who fronted the band for 10 years (1988–1998) and again from 2009 onward. "Epic" remains their biggest song, from Patton's first album with them. "He actually fell asleep on stage during an important showcase event."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 18 Bands Who Changed Lead Singers
facts.name: Faith No More

facts.title: MTV Racism Challenge (1983)
facts.body: CBS Records allegedly threatened to withdraw all their videos from MTV if the channel did not begin to feature Black artists. This action is credited with forcing MTV to cave and start showing videos from Michael Jackson's "Thriller" album, breaking the channel's unofficial color barrier. "It wasn't until CBS records allegedly threatened to pull all their videos from the channel that MTV caved and started to show videos from the thriller album."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: CBS Records (Canada)

facts.title: Pressure on MTV for Black Artist Airplay (1983)
facts.body: CBS Records reportedly threatened to withhold all their music videos from MTV unless the channel played Michael Jackson's early 1983 hit "Billie Jean." This legendary move is credited with forcing MTV, which had largely refused to play videos by black artists, to begin regularly rotating clips by black musicians. "Legend has it that the channel largely refused to play videos by black artists before CBS records threatened to withhold all of their videos unless MTV played Jackson's early 1983 hit Billy Jean."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1

facts.title: Grammy Win Controversy (1983)
facts.body: Toto's wins for "Toto IV" (Album of the Year) and "Rosanna" (Record of the Year) at the 1983 Grammys were highly controversial among 1980s rock critics, who cited them as evidence of the Recording Academy's "out of touchness." facts.title: Written by Accident, Recorded on LSD, Lost Money on Every Copy Sold
facts.body: New Order were devising a way to leave the stage early without audiences noticing, by running Stephen Morris's drum machine through the end of their set. They added sequenced keyboard parts and a bass line, and before long had the foundation of a complete song — all written by machines. The full recording session took place while the band was loaded on LSD; the engineers sent them to a café across the street to finish mixing in peace. During production, Gillian Gilbert accidentally missed programming one note in the melody, leaving it slightly out of time with the rhythm track — a mistake they kept because it sounded better. "Blue Monday" was released only as an 8-minute 12-inch single and became the best-selling 12-inch in music history. However, the elaborate die-cut packaging was so expensive to produce that New Order and the label lost money on every copy they sold. "New Order had the foundations of a new song, and it was all being played entirely by machines."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 6
facts.name: Blue Monday

facts.body: Joy Division had a pact: if anyone left for any reason, the band would break up. When singer Ian Curtis hanged himself from his kitchen doorframe on May 18, 1980 — the night before a North American tour that could have broken the band internationally — the three surviving members honored the dissolution but immediately reconstituted under the name New Order. Curtis was 23. After everyone took turns at vocals, guitarist Bernard Sumner was designated singer in late July 1980; Stephen Morris's girlfriend Gillian Gilbert was added on keyboards that fall, completing the classic lineup. "Blue Monday" — their biggest single — was built by accident from a drum machine left running while the band tried to leave the stage early; a missed programmed note became a happy accident. The most successful 12-inch in history, it lost money on every copy sold due to the expensive die-cut packaging. The name Blue Monday refers to the Monday after Ian Curtis died by suicide the previous Sunday. "New order made it cool to dance again."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: New Order's "Blue Monday" was released as an eight-minute, 12-inch single, gaining its biggest traction in dance clubs. facts.body: This iconic 8-minute 12-inch single originated from New Order's reluctance to perform encores. They devised a plan to turn on Stephen Morris's drum machine and walk off stage to drink backstage. The concept evolved with a sequencer triggering Gillian Welch's keyboards and Barney Sunder suggesting sequencing Peter Hook's bass lines, thus forming the entirely machine-played foundation of a new song. Legend has it the band, reportedly under the influence of LSD, recorded the tracks, after which the studio engineer, seeking peace, sent them to a cafe on Croc's Street to finish mixing. Upon its release, it gained radio play but had its most profound impact in dance clubs, dramatically shifting the landscape of dance music, making dancing "cool again," and forging crucial links between new music, rock, and dance. "Blue Monday" sold over 3 million copies, establishing it as the best-selling 12-inch record in the history of Planet Earth. Ironically, the elaborate artwork and cover for the single were so expensive to produce that New Order lost one pence on each copy sold, resulting in a total loss of 30,000 pounds for issuing "the world's favorite dance record." "Blue Monday sold over 3 million copies and it's still the best selling 12-inch record in the history of Planet Earth."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: "Thatchergate" Hoax (1983-1984)
facts.body: Following the Falklands War, this anarchist musical collective created a tape known as "Thatchergate." They cobbled together speeches from Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan to create what sounded like a fake phone call between the two leaders, including a fabricated discussion about firing missiles at allies. When the tape circulated in 1983, the US State Department suspected it was KGB disinformation, and MI6 considered it a possible Argentinian intelligence operation. Its true source was not discovered until January 1984. While not a song, its samples were used in tracks by Crass and the Dead Kennedys. Crass's motivation was to expose governments as "small-minded, petty and stupid," not just corrupt or violent, and the hoax indeed embarrassed the CIA. "The band cobbled together speeches from Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan into what appeared to be a fake phone call between the two of them."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Songs of Protest
facts.name: Crass

facts.title: Mighty Mighty Bosstones – Formed 1983 Boston; Invented Skacore by Mixing Two-Tone with Hardcore; Major Label by 1993
facts.body: The Mighty Mighty Bosstones came together in 1983 when a group of guys became obsessed with the Two-Tone sound despite some members playing in hardcore bands influenced by Motorhead and AC/DC. This combination of Two-Tone ska with American hardcore became known as skacore — annoying to ska purists and initially baffling to hardcore kids, but eventually it clicked. By 1993 they had a major label record deal and a signature look involving plaid suits. "The Boss Tones took two-tone style Skah and made it with American hardcore to create something that was eventually called Skahcore."

facts.title: Mother's Murder (March 3, 1983) – Boyfriend John "Dean" Ricardi Shot Connie and Friend, Caught via America's Most Wanted
facts.body: Dave Navarro was 15 years old when his mother Connie — one of the models on *Let's Make a Deal* with Monty Hall — was shot to death along with her best friend Sue by her ex-boyfriend, a bodybuilder named John Ricardi (who went by "Dean"). After the relationship deteriorated and Connie sought a restraining order, Ricardi broke into the house on the night of March 3, 1983, and waited. Dave narrowly escaped by spending the weekend with his father. Ricardi evaded capture for almost eight years until a tip from a viewer of *America's Most Wanted* led to his arrest in Houston, Texas, on January 4, 1991. Dave testified against him at trial; Ricardi was subsequently placed on death row at San Quentin. "Human beings are not equipped to know how to handle something like that."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Commercial Peak
facts.body: This album was conceived as a more commercially sounding record after Bowie's $17.5 million deal with EMI Records. Recorded with a new band of session players in just 17 days, including mixing, it was a massive and unexpected success, selling over six million copies and becoming Bowie's best-selling album of all time. Its hybrid rock dance funk sound was considered innovative for 1983. The album's success, however, caused Bowie to feel disconnected from his audience during the subsequent Serious Moonlight Tour. "Let's Dance was a massive success for Bowie and drew 2.6 million people to the serious Moonlight Tour as it wound through 16 countries."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This album, released in 1983, showcased a very dense and distorted guitar sound, aligning with a broader trend in music towards heavier sonic textures during that year. Its simultaneous release with R.E.M.'s *Murmur* illustrates the stark contrasts in guitar aesthetics present in the early 1980s. "sale el primer disco de Swans, el fifth."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El papel de REM en los '80
facts.name: Filth

facts.body: Released early in the band's career, this album, along with *Cop*, is today considered a true gem and a masterpiece of guitar sound experimentation. At the time of its release, Michael Gira was not a professional musician and had another job. It was released on independent labels and received little to no repercussion, selling very few copies and failing to gain recognition, making it difficult for the band to secure concerts. Critics gave it very bad reviews, finding it radically different from the mass-consumed rock of the early 80s by bands like Metallica and Iron Maiden. Its sound was completely atmospheric, contrasting with the sharp, virtuoso, and fast guitar playing common in 80s rock. The lyrics, penned by Michael Gira, were disturbing, addressing themes such as sex, religion, cruelty, submission (sometimes voluntary), love leading to submission, vile behaviors, and aggression. These lyrics were so powerful that, had the band been famous, they likely would have been censored. "Hoy en día esos dos trabajos están considerados, obras maestras de la experimentación del sonido de guitarra."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: SWANS. Una visión del rock diferente
facts.name: Filth

facts.body: This song reached number one on Billboard's Hot 100 for eight consecutive weeks, making it 1983's Top Hit and surpassing Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean." Sting wrote it about a stalker, though many listeners perceived it as an impassioned love song. By 2019, BMI recognized it as the most played song in radio history, largely due to Andy Summers' guitar arpeggio and Stuart Copeland's cracking snare drum rhythm. Its acclaimed music video featured the band depicted as jazzmen, bathed in shadow, in black and white. "every breath you take reached number one on Billboard's Hot 100, a song that its writer Sting called Evil and Sinister, spent eight weeks on top making it 1983's Top Hit."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: This song spent eight weeks at number one and is often mistaken for a love song, but songwriter Sting himself described it as "a fairly nasty song about surveillance and ownership and jealousy." It was an omnipresent, irresistible, and unavoidable hit, remarkably surpassing the success of Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" in a year flooded with "Thriller" hits. Fourteen years later, it spawned Puff Daddy's chart-topping homage to Biggie Smalls, "I'll Be Missing You." "Sting himself has called it, quote, a fairly nasty song about surveillance and ownership and jealousy."

facts.body: This song was the ubiquitous winner of the 1983 Billboard Song of the Summer. It is described as the "sultriest hit Sting ever wrote," originally an "ode to stalking and surveillance" that the public largely "mistook for a love song." The track's sound, characterized by Sting's moody bass line and Andy Summers' crackling guitar, is said to evoke a hot summer night. It holds the distinction of being the only Song of the Summer to be sampled in another year's Song of the Summer. "Even if it had had no lyrics, the police's biggest hit would sound like a hot summer night between Sting's moody bass line and Andy Summers crackling guitar."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: Released in 1983, this was Madonna's first full-length album. It followed the style of her relatively successful first two singles, "Everybody" and "Burning Up," being easygoing, disco-oriented, and lively. At this point, Madonna had not yet developed a strong personality, and her lyrics did not convey much depth. The album included "Borderline," which is noted as being slightly more feminist and more characteristic of her later style. "Son fáciles, son discotequeros, son movidos."

facts.title: Matricide and Incarceration (June 3, 1983)
facts.body: On June 3, 1983, under the delusion that his mother was Satan, a voice instructed Gordon to kill her. He fatally attacked her with a hammer and a butcher knife. He was sentenced to 16 years in jail, as California law prevented the use of insanity as a defense, though his schizophrenia was acknowledged by the judge. "On June 3, 1983, a voice told him to kill his mother because she was Satan in disguise."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Jim Gordon
